overview: The Belbullab-22 Starfighter is a starfighter whose design philosophy reflects the industrial and strategic priorities of Clone Wars (22–19 BBY). General Grievous flew a customized Belbullab-22 named Soulless One, outpacing clone interceptors. Production estimates place the class at ~800 units, though wartime losses, capture, and black-market duplication make precise fleet registries unreliable.
history:
Engineering teams first finalized the Belbullab-22 Starfighter blueprints during the political climate of Clone Wars (22–19 BBY). The starfighter was intended to solve specific fleet gaps—whether planetary assault, convoy escort, starfighter superiority, or terror bombardment—and shipwrights iterated hull plates, reactor output, and crew compartments accordingly.

Once deployed, the Belbullab-22 Starfighter appeared in fleet actions that defined its reputation. General Grievous flew a customized Belbullab-22 named Soulless One, outpacing clone interceptors. Combat logs show crews exploiting the class's strengths while improvising fixes for known weaknesses under fire, a pattern repeated across every major galactic conflict.

As doctrine evolved, rival factions studied captured Belbullab-22 Starfighter hulls. Refit yards duplicated weapons mounts and sensor suites; some variants never appeared in official manifests. Estimated production of ~800 units therefore understates how many similar silhouettes operated under alternate insignia.

Surviving Belbullab-22 Starfighter vessels now sit in museum orbits, mercenary fleets, and scrap worlds. Historians treat the class as a measure of how galactic wars industrialize violence—each hull a factory product that outlived the politicians who ordered it.
significance:
The Belbullab-22 Starfighter demonstrates how starfighter design shapes campaign outcomes. Its layout influenced successor programs and remains a case study in naval academies.

With roughly ~800 units hulls associated with Clone Wars (22–19 BBY), the class became a visual symbol of its faction's reach—recognizable in holonet footage and feared in convoy manifests.

Engineers still debate whether the Belbullab-22 Starfighter prioritized firepower over crew survival; that trade-off defines its legacy in both propaganda and honest after-action reports.
